name: Ugali with sukuma wiki
subtitle: The daily foundation of Kenyan life: a steaming mound of stiff white cornmeal paired with finely shredded collard greens sautéed with onions.

facts.label: Kind
facts.value: Stiff cornmeal porridge with braised greens

facts.label: Name meaning
facts.value: Sukuma wiki means 'push the week' or 'stretch the week' in Swahili

facts.label: Cooking utensil
facts.value: Mwiko, a flat wooden cooking spoon

parts.text: Ugali is the undisputed staple of Kenya, eaten across ethnic communities from the shores of Lake Victoria to the Indian Ocean coast.

It is made by gradually whisking coarse white cornmeal (unga wa mahindi) into boiling water, vigorously mashing and pressing the dough against the sides of the pot with a wooden paddle (mwiko) until it forms a dense, smooth, cohesive mound that pulls away from the metal.
It is virtually always accompanied by sukuma wiki: hearty collard greens finely shredded into thin ribbons and rapidly sautéed with sweet red onions, ripe tomatoes, vegetable oil, and salt.
The hot ugali is turned out onto a plate as a smooth dome.

Diners use the fingers of their right hand to pinch off a golf-ball-sized portion, knead it briefly in the palm to form a ball, press an indentation into it with the thumb, and use that edible spoon to scoop up the savory sukuma wiki, stew gravy, or grilled goat meat (nyama choma).
The phrase 'sukuma wiki' carries deep social significance: in Swahili, 'sukuma' means to push and 'wiki' means week.

Because collard greens grow rapidly year-round in kitchen gardens and are inexpensive in urban open-air markets, the vegetable was celebrated by working families as the food that 'pushes the week' forward until payday arrives.

blocks.title: Kenyan Ugali & Sukuma Wiki
blocks.sub: Everyday preparation as detailed by Kenya Tourism culinary archives and FAO food systems study.
blocks.note: Use white maize meal for traditional flavor and firm texture; keep collards slightly crisp rather than boiling into mush.

ingredients.name: water, brought to an active rolling boil
fresh collard greens (kale or sukuma wiki), washed and sliced very thin

steps.text: Bring water to a vigorous boil in a heavy cooking pot over high heat.
Slowly pour in half the cornmeal, stirring continuously with a wooden spoon (mwiko) as a thin porridge forms.
Gradually add the remaining flour while pressing and paddling the mixture against the sides of the pot to eliminate lumps.
Reduce heat to low, gather the dough into a center mound, cover the pot with a lid, and let it steam through until a toasted aroma appears.
In a separate pan, heat vegetable oil, sauté the diced red onions until golden, then add chopped tomatoes until soft.
Add the finely sliced collard greens and salt, tossing rapidly over high heat until wilted and bright green, retaining a gentle crunch.
Invert the ugali onto a plate, slice into wedges, and serve alongside the steaming sukuma wiki.

gaps: Nutritional debates comparing traditional stone-ground whole maize flour (unga wa kisiagi, high in fiber and germ) with industrialized sifted white flour (unga wa duka) in urban clinics.
The historical regional shift from indigenous sorghum and finger millet ugali to white cornmeal following British colonial agricultural marketing boards in the 1920s.
